items.body_md:
On August 8, Skillz Platform Inc., through Delaware counsel Sean Beach, filed three deposition notices targeting Oriel Bachar (Dkt. 54), Pinni Yaniv (Dkt. 55), and James Kong (Dkt. 53), each expressly framed as taken "in connection with the Chapter 15 petition for recognition of a foreign proceeding." Dkt. 52, a notice of service filed the same day, confirms that the deposition package was served on the relevant parties. The identity of James Kong and his relationship to the proceeding is not confirmed in available materials. Pinni Yaniv is Papaya's Israeli counsel at Meitar Law Offices, making him an obvious target for examination on the structure and bona fides of the Tel Aviv proceeding. Bachar, as co-founder and petitioner, is the primary factual witness on the assets, the proposed fund mechanism, and the claim that Israel constitutes the center of main interests.

The deposition campaign is Skillz's pre-recognition offensive, and its likely objectives are not difficult to read. Recognition as a foreign main proceeding under 11 U.S.C. § 1517 turns on whether the Israeli proceeding qualifies — and Skillz has every incentive to contest that characterization, to probe the adequacy of the court-supervised fund as creditor protection, and to develop a factual record for its objection brief, which is due August 27, 2026. That posture is consistent with the bench strength Skillz has assembled: Dkts. 50 and 51 added Latham & Watkins' Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo on pro hac vice motions filed August 7, bringing the Latham roster to five practitioners alongside local counsel Beach. This is not the profile of a party planning a perfunctory objection. Also worth noting: Papaya issued a public statement welcoming 
"the Delaware court's decision, which gives the company the certainty necessary to continue its regular operations until the recognition hearing"
 — a reference to Judge Walrath's temporary injunction reported by __[Calcalist / CTech](https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/idop8ipjs)__ on August 9, which stays collection and enforcement against U.S. assets pending the September 3 hearing.

The structural gap in the recovery picture is unchanged. 
Judge Cote ordered Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement, as well as approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and legal costs
, per __[Calcalist / CTech](https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/idop8ipjs)__. Against that, 
the proposed arrangement places available cash into a designated fund overseen by a court-appointed official, expected to contain around $100 million during 2026, along with additional annual contributions, which could support claim payments if the U.S. ruling is ultimately enforced in Israel
, per __[World Casino Directory](https://news.worldcasinodirectory.com/papaya-gaming-files-chapter-15-after-719m-verdict-123873)__. The deposition schedule adds procedural friction but does not move that ceiling. The next hard milestone is the objection deadline of August 27, 2026; the recognition hearing before Judge Walrath is set for September 3, 2026 at 9:30 AM (virtual).

items.body_md:
On August 7, an unidentified party filed Dkt. 98, an Objection, on the same day the deadline for objections to the bidding procedures and sale motion expired. 
Objections to the bidding procedures and sale motion were due August 7.
 The objecting party and the substance of Dkt. 98 are not confirmed from available docket text; what is confirmed is that at least one objection is now on record ahead of the August 14 hearing. Also filed August 7: Dkt. 99, a Document of unspecified type; Dkt. 97, reflecting the Meeting of Creditors under Chapter 11; and a Notice of Docketing Error with no docket number assigned. Dkt. 100, filed August 8 and logged as an Exhibit, remains the most recent entry and was covered in yesterday's briefing as likely supplementing the bidding-procedures record or responding to Dkt. 98 — that characterization is unconfirmed.

The more consequential open variable from yesterday's briefing has not resolved. 
Thor's no-cause diligence exit expired August 9, 2026.
 As of this briefing, no termination notice has appeared on the docket and no press report has confirmed either an exercise of that right or its waiver. Thor may transmit a termination notice directly to the debtors without an immediate docket filing, so the absence of a docket entry is not dispositive. What confirmation would look like: a docket-filed termination notice, a debtors' statement representing the purchase agreements remain operative, or a procedural filing at the August 14 hearing that proceeds on that assumption. Until one of those surfaces, the status of the stalking-horse commitment is unverified. 
That gap matters most for power: because the debtors contract through FlowX rather than directly with TNMP, the record does not yet establish which supply, scheduling, or interconnection agreements would transfer with the assets.
 The Assigned Contracts Schedule and proposed cure amounts — which would answer that question — 
are due August 21, 2026.



The court has scheduled the bidding-procedures and sale hearing for August 14 at 11 a.m. ET.
 That hearing will arrive with at least one live objection (Dkt. 98), an exhibit filing (Dkt. 100) whose relationship to that objection is unconfirmed, and no docket-confirmed representation that the stalking-horse agreements remain in effect. Whether Judge O'Hagan proceeds, adjourns, or takes the matter on a contested basis will depend on those facts as they stand Thursday morning. The recovery posture of the 11,700 wallet holders carrying $163,723,500 in unsecured IOU claims is entirely downstream of whether the bidding procedures are approved and a floor bid is in place to anchor the September process. 
The proposed downstream schedule calls for a September 8 qualified-bid deadline, a September 10 auction, and a September 16 sale hearing
 — none of which advances without a successful August 14 outcome. August 14 at 11 a.m. ET before Judge O'Hagan is the next concrete milestone.

items.body_md:
On August 8, the clerk docketed a BNC Certificate of Mailing at Dkt. 158, the sole filing to land since Friday's close. The certificate confirms that the court's noticing agent dispatched service on one or more of the documents filed August 7 — most likely the lift-stay motion at Dkt. 146 or the notices of appearance at Dkts. 147, 148, and 154, all of which require formal service under Bankr. S.D. Tex. local rules. A BNC certificate is purely administrative and carries no independent substantive weight; it is noted here because it closes the service loop on the August 7 cluster and starts the clock on any response period tied to those filings.

The lift-stay motion at Dkt. 146 therefore remains the live substantive issue. The movant's identity, the asset or claim at issue, and the relief sought have not been confirmed from a primary-source pull of the document, and that verification remains outstanding. What the BNC mailing certificate now establishes is that service has been completed, meaning the response clock — typically 14 days under Bankr. S.D. Tex. practice before Judge Lopez absent an agreed order — has begun to run. If the certificate reflects service executed on August 7, a response deadline of approximately August 21 would fall three days before the August 24 second-day hearing, creating a realistic scenario in which Dkt. 146 appears on that hearing agenda either as a contested matter or by agreed resolution. Whether the debtors and the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors (constituted August 6, Dkt. 137) file a joint opposition or proceed independently will be an early signal of how aligned estate interests and committee interests are on collateral perimeter questions. The two affidavits at Dkts. 156 and 157, also filed August 7, remain unconfirmed as to subject matter; they are most likely evidentiary support for either the lift-stay motion or the emergency motion at Dkt. 145, but neither interpretation should be treated as established until the documents are pulled.

The next concrete milestone is August 24, 2026 (Bankr. S.D. Tex., Case No. 26-90737, Judge Lopez, 1:00 p.m. CT): the second-day hearing at which interim first-day orders are expected to convert to final, the committee makes its first formal public appearance, and any unresolved lift-stay or emergency motion matter is likely to be addressed. The schedules of assets and liabilities and statements of financial affairs remain due September 23, 2026.
